v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version. Concepts: the catalog's w11 slugs, observer-pattern and delivery; no substitute needed. Setting from the Workshop bible v1.0.1 row ("an aquarium's closing routine"); the catalog's lld entries carry no setting, and w10's file does not exist yet, so the bible row was followed. Names: no renames inside this file; before use, two candidate aquarium names were dropped because each contained a place name from another case, and one candidate handle name because it contained a common first name. Options: the bible's third wrong option, restart the controller nightly, was left out (four options only). Sources: the Design Patterns book's own Observer entry could not be fetched, so the case quotes the univ-nantes catalogue (which credits Gamma et al., 1994), Wikipedia and the Node.js events documentation, each only as read.
title: The Doors That Didn't Lock

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. The closing routine I finished for an aquarium left its front doors unlocked all Tuesday night. Its log never says it tried to lock them.

blocks.text: My great-aunt Winifrith Torvaine built coin machines and clockwork figures for sixty years, and wrote small programs for local firms in her last ten. She died in the spring and left me her workshop of unfinished machines, each with a paper work order tied on with string. I program on night shifts, and I finish her machines at night.

This order came from Kelpmouth Aquarium. Its building controller is a small computer in the plant room that runs the lights, door locks and tank machinery. Winifrith had begun a library for it: a piece of code that other programs share.

When something happens, such as the aquarium closing, the controller announces it. That announcement is called an event. The last cleaner out presses closed on the panel by the staff door, at about 23:30 each night.

Jobs that want to hear an event sign up for it, like names on a list beside a doorbell. Each job is a subscriber. Announcing an event to every subscriber on its list is called publishing. Here is the list for aquarium closed, in order, each place counted from 0:

place 0  dim gallery lights
place 1  start feeding timer
place 2  test exit lights (once)
place 3  lock doors, arm alarm

The feeding timer tells the reef tanks' feeders when to drop food in the night. Place 2 was new. On Tuesday the electricians fitted new exit signs and asked for one test at closing, then never again. So the test, a run-once subscriber, takes itself off the list after it runs. That is called unsubscribing. I put it above the doors, because Winifrith's notes say the doors always go last.

Publishing walks the list in a loop: code that repeats the same steps. Here is publish. i is a place in the list. First i is 0. While i is less than the list's length, run the subscriber at place i, then add 1 to i. unsubscribe takes a subscriber out of that same list, the live list publish is walking:

publish(event):
  i = 0
  while i < length(list):
    list[i].run()
    i = i + 1
unsubscribe(s):
  remove s from list
Beside it Winifrith wrote: *The bell rings for everyone in the room. Someone always leaves while it is still ringing.*

The controller writes a log: one line for everything it does, with the time and what happened. The library went in on Thursday 1 October, and every closing since ended like Monday's. Here is Monday's closing, then Tuesday's:

23:24:16  aquarium closed
23:24:16  gallery lights dimmed
23:24:16  feeding timer started
23:24:16  doors locked, alarm armed

23:30:00  aquarium closed
23:30:00  gallery lights dimmed
23:30:00  feeding timer started
23:30:00  exit lights tested
23:30:00  unsubscribed: test exit lights

Nothing came after it. No alarm had been armed, so nothing rang all night. Muirne, the first keeper in, reads the log at 06:30 every morning, then walks the galleries. On Wednesday at 06:41, Muirne pushed a front door, and it swung open.
Nobody reads a log for the line that isn't there.

Bernadine, the operations manager, checked the cameras. The foyer stayed empty all night; nothing was touched. The electricians come back next Tuesday to fit fire doors, and want the same kind of one-time test. What should I change before then?

blocks.label: closing_tue_2330_redrawn.png
blocks.caption: I redrew Tuesday's closing at 23:30:00 as a sequence, read top to bottom. Publish runs places 0 and 1. At i = 2 the exit-light test runs, then unsubscribes, and the live list closes the gap: lock doors slides from place 3 to place 2. Publish adds 1, so i is 3, and the list is now 3 long. 3 is not less than 3, so the walk ends. Lock doors is never run.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: What you finished has an old name: the observer pattern, one of the design patterns (s5e06: named shapes of code for problems that keep coming back). One part keeps a list of who wants to hear, and tells each in turn. Getting one event to each of them is called delivery. Now walk your Tuesday by hand. For each time round, write down i, the list's length and what sits at each place. What is at place 2 just after the test takes itself off? Then ask your publish one more question: what would it do if a subscriber failed halfway, say the feeders didn't answer?

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: After the test takes itself off, the list is 3 long and lock doors has slid up to place 2. Then i becomes 3, and 3 is not less than 3, so the walk ends. And a failure: when a program can't do a step, it raises an error, which stops the code it is in. Nothing around run() catches one, that is, notices the error and carries on, so an error would stop publish on that line.

comments.author: u/never_unsubscribe_wulfrun
comments.text: The bug is letting a subscriber change the list it's being called from. Ban it. Make unsubscribe refuse, always. A run-once job keeps a flag, a yes-or-no value, called done: the first night it does its job and sets done to yes, and every night after it sees yes and does nothing. The list never changes, so nothing can ever slide. Simple rules beat clever code.

comments.author: u/backwards_loop_leofwine
comments.text: Old trick: walk the list backwards, from the last place down to place 0. When a subscriber takes itself out, only the places after it move up, and you've already been there. One line changes. Every list-walking loop I've fixed in twenty years got this fix.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Bernadine would rather have a queue (s5e06: a line where each job waits its turn). Publish would put one job per subscriber in it, and a worker, a small loop of its own, would take one job a second. If a job fails, the worker catches the error, writes it in the log and takes the next job. Bernadine says a few seconds before the doors lock is nothing.

reply.prompt: The electricians' fire-door test goes on the list next Tuesday. What should Odgerel change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Forbid unsubscribing: a run-once subscriber keeps a done flag and does nothing after.
options.verdict: The list holds; the walk still breaks
options.part2: I made unsubscribe refuse, and gave the fire-door test a done flag. On Winifrith's workbench I replayed 13 October first: all 4 subscribers ran and the doors locked at 23:30:00, with the test still on the list, done = yes. It went in on Wednesday. On Tuesday 20 October the electricians had unplugged the feeders' control box, and at 23:30:00 start feeding timer failed with the error feeders not answering. Nothing caught it, so publish stopped at place 1, with only the error in the log. The fire-door test and lock doors never ran. Muirne read the error at 06:30 and fed the reef tanks by hand, and at 06:41 found the front doors open again; the cameras show the foyer empty all night. And every finished one-time test will now sit on the list forever, doing nothing.
options.senior: Freezing the list does stop the slide, but it treats the symptom: the walk is still fragile, and it now breaks on the next thing that goes wrong, a failing subscriber. It also leaves every finished run-once job on the list for good, each checking a flag at every closing, which is how lists of listeners grow and leak. The library's job is to deliver safely while the list changes, not to forbid change.

options.text: Put each subscriber's delivery in a queue, and let one worker take one job a second.
options.part2: I gave the library a queue. Publish now puts one job per subscriber in it, in list order, and a worker takes one job a second. On the workbench, 13 October came out right: the test unsubscribed at 23:30:03 without touching the queue, and the doors locked at 23:30:04. It went in on Wednesday. On Tuesday 20 October the feeders' control box was unplugged, and at 23:30:02 the feeding job failed with the error feeders not answering. The worker caught it, logged it and took the next job: the fire-door test at 23:30:03, the doors at 23:30:04. Muirne read the error at 06:30 and fed the reef tanks by hand. But every night now the panel says closed while the doors stand unlocked for 4 s. And Bernadine asked what happens if someone presses open while closed's jobs are still waiting, so I had to write down an order for events as well as for subscribers.
options.senior: A queue gives each delivery its own job, so a removal can't shift anything and one failure can't stop the rest. It is a real design, and the right one when subscribers are slow or must survive a restart. The price is time and new questions: every subscriber now runs after its event, here 4 s for the doors, and you must state how jobs from different events are ordered. For four instant jobs on one controller, that is more machinery than the problem needs.

options.text: Walk the live list backwards, last place first, so a removal moves only places walked.
options.part2: I turned the walk round: i starts at the last place and counts down to 0. On the workbench, 13 October came out right: lock doors ran first at 23:30:00, then the test unsubscribed, and only places already walked moved. It went in on Wednesday. On Tuesday 20 October the feeders' control box was unplugged. The doors locked first and the fire-door test ran; then start feeding timer failed with the error feeders not answering, and nothing caught it. The walk stopped at place 1, so place 0, dim gallery lights, never ran. The galleries stayed at full light all night, shining into tanks whose fish are kept to a day and a night. Muirne turned the lights down at 06:30, read the error and fed the reef tanks by hand. The doors held.
options.senior: Walking backwards is a real trick, and it is safe for exactly one case: a subscriber removing itself. It reverses the order everyone was promised, so the doors now lock before the lights dim. A subscriber that removes an earlier one shifts the current one down, and it runs twice. And it does nothing about failures: one error still stops every subscriber not yet reached. It patches the walk rather than giving it rules.

options.text: Walk a copy of the list taken at publish time, and catch each subscriber's own error.
options.part2: Publish now copies the list first and walks the copy, and each subscriber's run is wrapped so its error is caught, logged with its name, and the walk goes on. On the workbench, 13 October came out right: all 4 ran at 23:30:00, the test unsubscribed from the live list, and the copy still had lock doors at place 3. It went in on Wednesday. On Tuesday 20 October the feeders' control box was unplugged, and start feeding timer failed with the error feeders not answering. It was caught and logged; the fire-door test ran and took itself off; the doors locked and the alarm armed at 23:30:00. Muirne read the error at 06:30 and fed the reef tanks by hand. I wrote the rules beside Winifrith's line: a subscriber removed during delivery still gets that event, one added during delivery waits for the next, and the order is the list's.
options.senior: Deliver to a snapshot: the list as it stood when the event was published. Unsubscribing and subscribing then change only the live list, so nothing slides under the walk, and the rules can be stated in one sentence each. Wrapping each call keeps one subscriber's failure its own problem, while the error is still reported. Delivery stays immediate and in a stated order. It is what Node's own event emitter does about removals, and what a library should write down before anyone relies on it.

sim.title: Replay the closing on Winifrith's workbench
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying one closing from 23:29:50, before the event. At 23:30:00 aquarium closed is published to 4 subscribers, in order: place 0 dim gallery lights, place 1 start feeding timer, place 2 a run-once test, place 3 lock doors, arm alarm. Each job is instant, and the run-once test unsubscribes as its last act, which changes the live list. Pick the night: Tuesday 13 October (test exit lights) or Tuesday 20 October (test fire doors, and the feeders' control box unplugged, so start feeding timer fails with an error). Pick a design: as built, walking the live list; no unsubscribing, with a done flag; walking the live list backwards; a queue whose one worker takes one job a second from 23:30:01; or walking a copy taken at publish time, with each error caught.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press step four times and read place 2's line, then play the closing. Try no unsubscribing, then backwards, then the queue, and read when the doors lock. Then the copy. Now switch the night to 20 October and run all five again: which designs still lock the doors, and what happens to the gallery lights?

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke and nobody touched the doors. The run-once test took itself off the very list publish was walking, lock doors slid up into the place the walk had just passed, and the walk ended one subscriber short.

steps.title: Tuesday's walk, one pass at a time.
steps.text: First, with i = 0, dim gallery lights ran. Second, with i = 1, start feeding timer ran. Third, with i = 2, test exit lights ran, then unsubscribed; removing it closed the gap in the live list, so lock doors moved from place 3 to place 2. Fourth, publish added 1, so i was 3, but the list was now 3 long, and 3 < 3 is false, so the walk ended. Lock doors never ran, the alarm was never armed, and nothing rang. From 1 to 12 October the list held three subscribers and none of them unsubscribed, so every walk ran clean. Had the test been put last, nothing would have been skipped; the subscriber right behind a self-removing one is skipped, and Winifrith's notes put the doors last.

steps.title: The observer pattern leaves a question open.
steps.text: In the observer pattern, one object, the subject, keeps a list of the parts that want to hear, its observers or subscribers, and tells each in turn when something happens. The pattern as written in Design Patterns leaves out unsubscribing, and so it never says what a delivery owes a list that changes while it is being walked. A library has to answer four questions in writing: in what order subscribers hear, what a subscriber removed during delivery gets, what one added during delivery gets, and what happens when one fails. Winifrith's library answered none of them, so the loop answered them by accident.

steps.title: Deliver to a copy.
steps.text: First, publish copies the list as it stands: a snapshot. Second, it walks the copy, in the copy's order. Third, any unsubscribe or subscribe during the walk changes only the live list, so the copy cannot slide. Fourth, the next publish copies the list again, with the change in it. The rules then say themselves: a subscriber removed during delivery still gets this event, one added during delivery waits for the next, and the order is the list's. Node's event emitter works the same way: listeners attached when the event was emitted are all called, even if one is removed mid-call. What can go wrong: a subscriber removed mid-delivery runs once more, so one that must stop at once should check its own state when it runs.

steps.title: Catch each subscriber's error.
steps.text: Wrap each call in its own catch: run the subscriber; if it raises an error, write the error in the log with the subscriber's name; then go on to the next. One failing feeder then costs the feed, not the doors. The error must still be reported, not swallowed: on 20 October it was the first line Muirne read at 06:30. What can go wrong: a caught error in a log nobody reads is just a quieter Tuesday, so send failures where a person will see them in time.

steps.title: Why not the others?
steps.text: Forbidding unsubscribing keeps the list still, but every finished run-once job stays on it forever, and a failing subscriber still stops the walk: on 20 October the doors stayed unlocked again. Walking backwards is safe only for a subscriber removing itself; it reverses the order, makes a subscriber that removes an earlier one run twice, and still stops at an error: on 20 October the gallery lights stayed at full all night. A queue with one worker is safe and isolates each job, but every subscriber now runs after its event, the doors 4 s late, and the order of jobs across events has to be stated too.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed for Tuesday 20 October at 23:30:00. The event aquarium closed goes to publish, which copies the live list and walks the copy of 4 places. The fire-door test unsubscribes from the live list, which is now 3 long; the copy is unchanged. The feeding timer's error is caught and logged. Lock doors at place 3 runs, and the doors lock at 23:30:00.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for Tuesday 20 October. Publish copies the live list at 23:30:00 and walks the copy. When the fire-door test unsubscribes, only the live list changes, so lock doors stays at place 3 of the copy and runs. The feeding timer's error is caught and logged, and the walk goes on. The doors lock at 23:30:00.

fix.title: The fix: walk a copy, catch each error, write the rules down
fix.text: Change publish to copy the subscriber list first and walk the copy, in list order. Leave subscribe and unsubscribe changing only the live list. Wrap each subscriber's run so an error is caught, logged with the subscriber's name and sent where a keeper will see it, and the walk goes on. Then write the four rules beside Winifrith's line: subscribers hear in list order; one removed during delivery still gets that event; one added during delivery waits for the next; one that fails is reported and does not stop the rest. Add two tests: a run-once subscriber followed by one that must still run, and a failing subscriber followed by one that must still run.

limits: A subscriber removed during delivery still gets the event it is being removed from. That is usually right, and Node does the same, but a subscriber that must stop at once has to check its own state when it runs.
Catching an error helps only if someone reads it. A caught error in a log nobody opens is a quieter version of Tuesday; send failures where a person will see them in time.
Delivery is still one subscriber after another: a slow subscriber holds up every one behind it. Anything slow, such as sending a report by email, belongs on a queue of its own.

Good
Bad
rows: As built: walk the live list
Short, and right while nobody unsubscribes.
A run-once subscriber shifts the next one past the walk: the doors unlocked all night. An error stops the rest.
Finished run-once jobs stay forever; on 20 October the feeders' error stops the walk and the doors stay unlocked.
Safe when a subscriber removes itself; the doors lock first.
Reverses the order; removing an earlier subscriber runs one twice; on 20 October the lights stay full all night.
Each job alone: removals and errors can't stop the rest.
Every subscriber runs late, the doors 4 s after the event; the order across events must be stated.
Walk a copy, catch each error
All 4 run at 23:30:00 on both nights; the rules fit in four lines.
A removed subscriber still gets the current event; a slow one still holds up the rest.

explain.seniorTake: A publish-and-subscribe library is a promise to people who never read its code: every subscriber that was listening hears the event, in an order you can state, whatever the others do. Two things break that promise quietly. A list that changes while it is walked, because subscribers come and go from inside the walk, and one subscriber's failure becoming everyone's. Deliver to a snapshot and wrap each call, and both become rules you can write in a sentence. Then write them down: order, removals during delivery, additions during delivery, failures. Anything that keeps a building safe should not depend on where it happens to sit in a list.

realWorld.title: Node.js: removals don't touch an emit in progress
realWorld.text: The Node.js events documentation: "Once an event is emitted, all listeners attached to it at the time of emitting are called in order. This implies that any removeListener() or removeAllListeners() calls after emitting and before the last listener finishes execution will not remove them from emit() in progress." Its example comment reads "callbackA removes listener callbackB but it will still be called."

realWorld.title: Node.js: one-time listeners and order
realWorld.text: The same page: "The EventEmitter calls all listeners synchronously in the order in which they were registered." Of once(): "Adds a one-time listener function for the event named eventName. The next time eventName is triggered, this listener is removed and then invoked." Removed first, then called: a run-once subscriber done safely.

realWorld.title: Node.js: one listener's error, two answers
realWorld.text: For EventTarget, the same page says: "Throwing within an event listener will not stop the other registered handlers from being invoked." That is a stated rule for EventTarget; a library like Winifrith's has to state its own, and catch each error in its own code.

realWorld.title: Observer, as the catalogue words it
realWorld.text: The univ-nantes pattern catalogue, which credits Design Patterns (Gamma et al.), gives the intent: "An observer defines a dependency relationship between objects so that, when the state of an object changes, all its dependents are automatically notified and updated." Among the consequences it lists "Unexpected updates".

realWorld.title: A Gang of Four pattern, with gaps on purpose
realWorld.text: Wikipedia: the subject "maintains a list of its dependents" and notifies them, and the pattern is "listed among the 23 well-known "Gang of Four" design patterns". It adds: "The observer pattern, as formalized in Design Patterns, deliberately omits concerns such as unsubscription," leaving those to the library.

asked: Design a small publish-and-subscribe (event bus) library.
What happens if a listener unsubscribes while an event is being delivered?
How do you stop one bad listener from breaking the others?
interview.answer: I'd keep, per event name, a list of subscribers, with subscribe returning a handle to unsubscribe, and a once option. The core decision is the delivery contract, written down: subscribers are called in the order they subscribed; delivery goes to a snapshot of the list taken at publish time, so a subscriber removed during delivery still gets the current event and one added during delivery waits for the next; and each call is wrapped so a subscriber's error is caught, reported with its name, and doesn't stop the rest. The snapshot is what stops the classic bug, where a once listener removes itself from the live list mid-loop and the next listener slides into the place the loop just passed and is skipped. Walking backwards or banning unsubscription are patches: one reverses the order, the other leaks finished listeners and still dies on the first error. I'd also say whether delivery is synchronous. Synchronous is simple and immediate but a slow subscriber delays the others; a queue per subscriber or an async hand-off isolates slow ones at the cost of delay and a rule for ordering across events. Re-entrancy needs a rule too: if a subscriber publishes another event, does it run at once, nested, or after the current delivery? Tests: a self-removing subscriber followed by one that must run, a throwing subscriber followed by one that must run, and a subscriber added mid-delivery that must not run until the next event.

atWork: Look for code that keeps a list of listeners, handlers, callbacks or subscribers and walks it: an event bus, a plugin system, the change listeners on a screen. Read-only access to the code is enough. For each, check three things. Does the walk go over a copy, or over the live list that unsubscribe and once() change? Is each call wrapped, so one listener's error is caught and reported rather than stopping the rest? Is the delivery order written down, along with what a listener added or removed during delivery gets? Then add two tests: a listener that removes itself, followed by one that must still run; and a listener that fails, followed by one that must still run. Where a listener does safety work, such as locking, alarms or payments, don't let it depend on its place in a list: check afterwards that it ran, and raise an alert when it didn't. Writing these rules down now costs less than finding them in an incident review later.

recall.prompt: Your team's online shop publishes order placed to a list of subscribers: send the receipt, reserve the stock, a run-once welcome discount that unsubscribes itself, then tell the warehouse. Publish walks the list with a counter. On the day the welcome discount was added, the warehouse never heard about the first order, and the logs show no error. What happened, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The run-once subscriber removed itself from the list being walked; the rest moved up a place, so the next one was skipped
Deliver to a copy of the list taken at publish time; unsubscribing changes only the live list
State the rules: a subscriber removed during delivery still gets this event, one added waits for the next

recall.model: The welcome discount unsubscribed itself from the very list publish was walking. Removing it closed the gap, so tell the warehouse moved up into the place the counter had just passed; the counter went on past the end of the shorter list, and the warehouse was skipped. No error, because nothing failed. Change publish to walk a copy of the list taken at publish time, a snapshot, so unsubscribing changes only the live list and nothing slides under the walk. Then state the rules: a subscriber removed during delivery still gets this event, one added during delivery waits for the next event, and subscribers hear in list order.

recall.prompt: Publish walks the live list [A, B, C, D] with i from 0, adding 1 after each run. B is a run-once subscriber that unsubscribes itself when it runs. Which subscribers run?
recall.why: At i = 1, B runs and removes itself, so C moves to place 1 and D to place 2. Publish then sets i to 2, which is D. C, which slid into the place just passed, never runs.

recall.prompt: A colleague's smart-home hub delivers motion detected to its subscribers by walking a copy of the list. One subscriber, which turns on the porch light, fails when the bulb's controller is offline, and the hub stops there: the camera and the phone message behind it never run. Your colleague suggests moving the porch light to the end of the list. What do you say, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Moving it only moves the problem: whichever subscriber fails next stops everyone behind it
Catch each subscriber's error and carry on to the next
Report the caught error where a person sees it, rather than swallowing it

recall.model: Moving the porch light only moves the problem: whichever subscriber fails next, the camera one day or any subscriber added later, still stops everyone after it. The fix belongs in the hub's delivery: wrap each subscriber's call so its error is caught, logged with the subscriber's name, and delivery carries on to the next. Then report the caught error where a person will see it, a message to the owner, rather than swallowing it, so the offline bulb still gets fixed.

recall.prompt: In Node.js, while an event is being emitted, one listener removes another listener of the same event that has not run yet. Is the removed listener called in that emit?
options: No, it is dropped at once
Yes: every listener attached when the emit began is called; the removal counts from the next emit
Only if it was added with once()
It depends on the order they were added in
recall.why: Node's documentation says all listeners attached at the time of emitting are called in order, and a removeListener() during the emit does not remove them from the emit in progress. It delivers to a snapshot; the removal takes effect from the next event.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Publish walks a copy and catches each error, and every door has locked since October. In January Bernadine asked for a night report: a new subscriber that emails the day's visitor numbers to the director. Following Winifrith's notes, I put it above the doors. On Tuesday 12 January the mail server was slow, and the report took 90 s to send. Nothing failed. The log says aquarium closed at 23:30:00 and doors locked, alarm armed at 23:31:30.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the doors lock 90 s late when nothing failed, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Delivery is one subscriber after another: a slow one holds up everyone behind it
Move slow work off the walk: hand the email to a queue or background job, or give it a time limit
State the order on purpose: safety subscribers such as the doors first, not last by habit

coldCase.model: Catching errors isolates failures, not slowness. Delivery still runs one subscriber after another, so lock doors waits for the report to finish: 90 s of email held up everyone behind it, and the doors stood unlocked from 23:30:00 to 23:31:30. Move slow work off the walk: the report subscriber should hand the email to a queue of its own, with its own worker, or to a background job, and return at once; give it a time limit as well. And state the order on purpose rather than by habit: put the doors first, so locking never waits for anything, and check afterwards that the doors locked.
